name: Nikhil Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a dozer at Sorrel Flat, a big open-pit lithium mine. I push up the blasted rock for the loaders, build the dump edges and clean up the benches so everything's safe and tidy. I'm on five days, two off, then nights. What I love is a good clean push, when the blade's full and the ground's flat behind you, and what wears me out is sitting there on a night shift waiting for a broken-down loader.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner, Anjali, in a rented place in Carvin. She works at the bank branch on the main street. Last year I bought a second-hand skid-steer, a little loader, on a loan, and I do weekend jobs with it: driveways, house pads, clearing blocks. That's why there's hardly anything in savings, maybe a week or two, it all goes on the loan. I use AI every day, for quoting jobs, for my books, even for working out the best dozer push on a tricky slope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fine by me. Slow and steady suits a small business guy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now people can stop panicking and get back to work. At work I'd show the guys how I use AI for my quotes, because even the small stuff saves time. I don't argue online, waste of energy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my plan works. I keep the mine job for steady pay and grow the skid-steer business on weekends. In five years I want two machines and a pickup with my name on the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep my shifts, keep taking weekend jobs, pay the loan off early if I can, maybe by next spring. I'd keep using AI for the paperwork side, quotes, invoices, the tax stuff. Then save for a second machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Actually pretty good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where did the business idea come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad runs the hardware shop on the main street in Carvin. I grew up watching him open at seven every morning and know every customer by name. I want that, being your own boss and being trusted in the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Anjali think of the weekend business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She thinks I'm crazy and she does my books with me on Sunday night. She's the careful one, she makes sure the loan payment comes out before anything else. Good team.

S0.say: He'd say people can stop panicking and get back to work, and would show colleagues how he uses AI for quotes. He doesn't argue online.
S0.think: He thinks his plan works in this picture: steady mine pay plus a growing weekend skid-steer business, aiming for two machines in five years.
S0.do: Keeps his shifts and weekend jobs, aims to pay off the loan early by next spring and uses AI for quotes, invoices and tax. Then saves for a second machine.
S0.quote: In five years I want two machines and a pickup with my name on the door.
S0.fieldNote: Nikhil's goal is ownership: a small earthmoving business modelled on his father's hardware shop. His thin savings are tied up in a machine loan, not consumption. He uses AI as a practical business tool every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I'd bet on, honestly. And I think I could do well in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is coming, so get in front of it. People who learn the new tools will be fine. I'd say it at work, but I'd also say the company should run apprenticeships, not leave the young ones behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the dozer job shrinks, because remote and auto dozers are already a thing. But the weekend business could grow, because small jobs on house blocks are too fiddly for big companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my hand up for the remote dozer training at the mine straight away, to keep the wage going. On the business, I'd fit a GPS grade control kit to the skid-steer, which is a system that guides the blade to the exact level, so I can quote faster and work more accurately. I'd push to grow the weekend work into something I could do full-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. Like the night before your first day somewhere new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The grade control kit costs money and you've got a week or two saved. How would you pay for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably on the same loan, extended. Anjali would hate it. I'd show her the numbers, and if the jobs pay it off in a year, she'd let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older guys who can't type. I'd help where I can, but I also think a man has to step up. Nobody's going to hand you a new career.

S1.say: He'd say change is coming so people should get in front of it by learning the new tools, while calling for the company to run apprenticeships for young workers.
S1.think: He expects the dozer job to shrink with remote and autonomous dozers, but thinks his weekend business could grow because small house-block jobs are too fiddly for big companies.
S1.do: Takes remote dozer training immediately to keep the wage, and adds a GPS grade control kit to his skid-steer, financed by extending the loan. Aims to grow the weekend work into a full-time business.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, like the night before a new job.
S1.quote: Nobody's going to hand you a new career.
S1.fieldNote: Nikhil sees steady change as a chance to grow his own business, and he's ready to bring automation into it. He'd take on more debt with thin savings, relying on his partner to check the numbers. His traditional outlook shows in self-reliance and support for apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That one's not so fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the market will sort it out eventually, but it'll be rough for a while, so look after your family and your town. I wouldn't be asking for handouts, I'd be asking for less red tape so people can start new things fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be worried. If robots can do house pads too, then my little business is up against machines that don't sleep. And I've got a loan on a skid-steer that suddenly isn't worth much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the skid-steer in the first month while it's still worth something and clear the loan. I'd keep the mine job as long as it lasted. Then I'd look for work setting up or servicing the robot machines, or help my dad at the shop, because a hardware store still needs someone to know the customers, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My stomach drops when I think about selling the machine. But I'd still feel like I could do something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does selling the skid-steer mean to you, beyond the money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's my name, really. It's the first thing I ever owned that made money. Selling it would feel like giving up, even if it was the smart move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the two years give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just enough time to get out of debt and get my feet under me. Not enough time to build anything. You'd be playing defence the whole time.

S2.say: He'd say the market will sort it out eventually but it'll be rough, so people should look after family and town, and he'd ask for less red tape rather than handouts.
S2.think: He's worried that robots could take house-pad work too, leaving his small business competing with machines that never sleep and a loan on a machine losing value.
S2.do: Sells the skid-steer in the first month to clear the loan and keeps the mine job as long as it lasts. Then looks for robot setup or servicing work or helps at his father's hardware shop.
S2.feel: Anxious, with his stomach dropping at the idea of selling the machine, but still feeling able to act.
S2.quote: It's the first thing I ever owned that made money. Selling it would feel like giving up, even if it was the smart move.
S2.fieldNote: Two years turns Nikhil from building to defending, and the hardest step for him is selling his machine. He keeps his free-market view, asking for less red tape rather than support. His father's shop becomes his family safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's something I could work with, if I'm smart about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead if you start now, so don't wait. I'd probably talk about it at the business group Dad goes to, the local traders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I could ride the wave. The years before AGI arrives would be full of work setting up new machines and preparing sites, and I'd want my business doing that work. After 2031, I'd have to see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd fit the grade control kit to the skid-steer and start bidding on site preparation for the new automated mine areas, small jobs the big contractors don't want. I'd keep the mine job until the business could pay me. I'd also put every spare dollar against the loan, so I'm not carrying debt into 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Good uneasy, mostly. Like going fast on a road you know well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd bid on work for the automated areas. Doesn't that speed up the thing that takes jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I see it. But if I don't do it, someone from the city will. I'd rather the money stay in Carvin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the business in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably I'd have to sell, or switch to running robot machines myself as a contractor. Either way, I'd want it debt-free so I'm selling something, not owing something.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough to get ahead if people start now, and would talk about it at the local traders' group his father attends.
S3.think: He thinks he could ride the wave of setup and site preparation work before AGI arrives, but would have to see what happens after 2031.
S3.do: Fits the grade control kit and bids on small site preparation jobs for the new automated mine areas. Keeps the mine job until the business can pay him and puts every spare dollar against the loan.
S3.feel: Uneasy in a mostly good way, like driving fast on a familiar road.
S3.quote: But if I don't do it, someone from the city will. I'd rather the money stay in Carvin.
S3.fieldNote: Nikhil openly accepts that his business would help build the automation that threatens jobs, reasoning that the money should stay local. He plans to be debt-free before 2031. His mood is uneasy but energised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Now that's a business plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse not to prepare. Learn, save, build something. I'd tell the young guys on the crew to get a trade or start something now, not in 2035.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well for most of the ten years. Two machines, maybe three, then probably running autonomous gear myself as a contractor. The last stretch is anyone's guess, but I'd have assets by then, not just a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, pay the loan down, fit the grade control kit and go part-time at the mine once the weekend business covers half my wage. I'd use AI for all my quoting and scheduling. I'd talk to Anjali about getting married in the next couple of years, because with ten years I'd feel safe enough to plan that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. The ending's the same, but I'd meet it as an owner, not an employee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the ending's the same. Why calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if the machines do all the work, I'd rather be the guy who owns a few of them. That's the same thing my dad would say about the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years change compared with the 2028 picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 I'm selling my skid-steer to pay the bank. In 2036, I'm buying my third machine. It's the difference between losing your start and building on it.

S4.say: He'd say there's no excuse not to prepare and would urge young crew members to get a trade or start something now rather than in 2035.
S4.think: He expects to do well for most of the decade, growing to two or three machines and then running autonomous gear as a contractor, with assets rather than just a wage by the end.
S4.do: Pays down the loan, fits the grade control kit and goes part-time at the mine once the business covers half his wage. Uses AI for quoting and scheduling and plans to marry his partner within a couple of years.
S4.feel: Calm, because he'd meet the same ending as an owner rather than an employee.
S4.quote: Because if the machines do all the work, I'd rather be the guy who owns a few of them.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years fits Nikhil's ownership plan perfectly, and he stays calm even about full AGI. He links his thinking directly to his father's shop. This is also the only picture where he feels safe enough to plan a wedding.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd lose the machine and the start I've built. What would help is less red tape for small businesses and fair access to the new machines, so it's not just the big companies who can afford them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about small towns and ownership. If the machines are all owned by big companies in the city, the money leaves. If some are owned by people like me, it stays.

headlineQuote: It's the difference between losing your start and building on it.
portrait: Nikhil Patel is a 27-year-old dozer operator at the Sorrel Flat lithium mine, renting in Carvin with his partner Anjali, who works at the bank, and running a weekend skid-steer business on a loan that eats his savings. He's traditional and enterprising, inspired by his father's hardware shop, and uses AI every day for quotes and books. He's calm in a plateau and in steady change, where he'd bring automation into his own business. AGI in two years makes him anxious because he'd have to sell his machine, but five and ten years let him build an ownership plan and even plan a wedding. He wants less red tape and fair access to new machines.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd lose his machine and the start he has built.
whatWouldHelp: Less red tape for small businesses and fair access to the new machines, so not only big companies can afford them.
